title: Room-temperature graphene sub-terahertz detector integrated on a silicon dielectric waveguide
authors: A. Titchenko, K. Shein, M. Titova, M. Kashchenko, O. Popova, R. Izmaylov, E. I. Titova, I. Gayduchenko, G. Goltsman
abstract: Terahertz (THz) photonics offers a promising platform for next-generation 6G wireless communications, on-chip spectrometers, and non-invasive biomedical sensors. In the near- and mid-infrared, monolithically integrated photodetectors are a cornerstone of photonic integrated circuits (PICs). In the THz range, however, such integration on low-loss dielectric waveguides remains an open challenge: to date, room-temperature on-waveguide detection has been realized only through hybrid flip-chip assembly of discrete elements, which leads to poor mode coupling, larger footprint, and reduced mechanical stability. Here we address this gap by demonstrating a room-temperature graphene sub-THz detector monolithically integrated on a high-resistivity silicon dielectric waveguide for D-band (110-170 GHz) operation. We couple an hBN-encapsulated graphene channel to the guided mode using a tapered slot-line antenna patterned directly onto the silicon surface. The detector achieves a voltage responsivity of 11.5 V/W and a 3 dB bandwidth of 1.94 GHz, with the latter currently limited by parasitic inductance of the readout interconnects rather than by the intrinsic graphene response. This platform provides a practical pathway to fully integrated room-temperature THz photonic circuits, where electrostatic gating and impedance matching can improve both responsivity and bandwidth by roughly an order of magnitude.
summary: This paper reports the successful demonstration of a room-temperature, monolithic graphene sub-THz detector integrated directly onto a silicon dielectric waveguide. By coupling the guided THz mode via a patterned antenna, the authors achieved high responsivity, establishing a practical platform for fully integrated THz photonic circuits. This work addresses a major technological bottleneck in on-chip THz detection.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is achieving room-temperature, monolithic integration of sub-terahertz detectors directly onto low-loss dielectric waveguides, overcoming limitations associated with hybrid assembly methods.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a room-temperature, monolithic graphene sub-THz detector on a silicon waveguide, achieving a voltage responsivity of 11.5 V/W and a 3 dB bandwidth of 1.94 GHz.
method: The detection relies on coupling the guided THz mode to an hBN-encapsulated graphene channel using a tapered slot-line antenna patterned directly onto the silicon surface.
model_or_system: The platform utilizes a high-resistivity silicon dielectric waveguide with an Effective-Dielectric-Medium (EDM) cladding. The detection mechanism is bolometric, measuring the photoresponse of the graphene to the evanescent waveguide mode.
key_observables: Voltage responsivity (11.5 V/W), 3 dB bandwidth (1.94 GHz), Temperature Coefficient of Resistance (0.18% K^-1), and Noise-Equivalent Power (2.46 nW/Hz^1/2).
important_parameters: Operating band: D-band (110–170 GHz); Operating frequency: 139 GHz; The bandwidth is currently limited by parasitic readout inductance.
main_assumptions: The EDM cladding model is assumed valid in the long-wavelength regime; the measured bandwidth is attributed to external readout parasitics, not the intrinsic graphene response.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the device design, field distribution, and S-parameters. Figure 2 shows electrical characterization, including the I-V curve, temperature dependence of resistance, and photoresponse measurements.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup, presents the measured and simulated S-parameters and electrical transport characteristics, and concludes by discussing the device's potential for fully integrated THz photonic circuits.
why_interesting: While focused on photonics and solid-state devices, the work demonstrates advanced integration techniques and characterization of nanoscale electronic components (graphene) coupled to electromagnetic waves, which has parallels with quantum optics and open quantum systems research.
